newsitem.title: CHINA: China's president promises HK autonomy and freedom.
newsitem.headline: China's president promises HK autonomy and freedom.

text.p: China's president and Hong Kong's new leader pledged on the first day of Beijing's rule on Tuesday that this former British colony would remain economically powerful with autonomy and existing freedoms.
Their twin reassurance on the future of democracy here came hours after Hong Kong returned to China ending 156 years of British rule.
Thousands of Chinese troops poured across the border in a demonstration of the historic sovereignty transfer.
Hong Kong's 6.4 million population, 98 percent Chinese, acclaimed a return to the motherland amid uncertainty about the future of civil liberties under communist rule.

The declarations by China's President Jiang Zemin and Hong Kong's newly-inaugurated leader Tung Chee-hwa clearly aimed at easing both local anxieties and fears constantly expressed by Western leaders.
Jiang told Hong Kong residents that a promised high degree of self-rule would be honoured for this capitalist East Asian economic hub -- now the richest city in China.

"There is no reason to change, the one-country, two-systems, Hong Kong people ruling Hong Kong, the high degree of autonomy...all these will be long-term directions (governing Hong Kong)," Jiang said in a speech during an inauguration ceremony of the new Hong Kong government as part of China.
Jiang reiterated the words of China's late paramount leader about Hong Kong. "Mr Deng Xiaoping said it well. Hong Kong people can rule Hong Kong well. We must have confidence."
He also said that eventually, Taiwan would be reunified with China. "Hong Kong, Macau and Taiwan will be reunited together with China," he said, without elaboration.
Portuguese-administered Macau will revert to China in 1999.

Deng, who died in February, was responsible for the principle of Hong Kong's return to communist-ruled China under a "one country, two systems" formula, allowing the territory to keep its freewheeling capitalist lifestyle for 50 years.
Tung Chee-hwa, China's anointed Chief Executive, said existing freedoms in Hong Kong would continue.

"We will protect the lifestyle of Hong Kong people. They will continue to fully enjoy freedom of speech, association, press, political and civil liberties as guaranteed by international covenants," Tung said.
"Democracy is an important facet of the modern society," he said, adding that all lawful organisations would be allowed to air their views.
They spoke a few hours after a midnight ceremony when Britain's royal heir Prince Charles handed this "Pearl of the Orient" back to China which lost the territory in 19th century Opium Wars.
Jiang told the government ceremony: "After Hong Kong returns to the motherland, the overwhelming majority of the laws previously in force will be maintained.
"Hong Kong residents will enjoy their rights and freedoms in accordance with law and all will be equal before the law."

Jiang said Hong Kong would retain the status of a free port and an international financial, trade and shipping centre, while keeping ties with other countries and organisations, "so that this international economic metropolis will forever be vigorous and dynamic."
Foreigners could live and work here "in peace and contentment." The law would protect private property, trade activities and the investment interests of other countries."
"With the continuous advance of China's modernisation drive, Hong Kong's economic link with the mainland will become even closer and its role as a bridge will be increasingly enhanced."

Tung, in his speech said the new Basic Law spelt out how Hong Kong differed from China. "It clearly prescribes the social, economic and political systems in Hong Kong which are different from those in the mainland," Tung said.
"It protects the rights and lifestyles of the Hong Kong people and delineates our obligations."
